At today's "Surprise and Shine" event, Apple confirmed the rollout timeline for the new Siri AI, which will launch first in English and then expand to five additional languages in October. Here are the details.

Siri AI language expansion confirmed for October rollout

In addition to unveiling the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple today also announced its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. The company also launched the Apple Watch Series 12 Ultra 4, as well as the AirPods 5 with active noise cancellation.

The common thread among these devices is that they all rely on one or more features of the new Siri AI—which delivers a more powerful large language model assistant through Apple's partnership with Google.

Following the initial reveal of Siri AI at this year's WWDC, Apple today provided further details on the specific rollout plan for the languages it will support.

Apple's VP of Product Marketing for AI, Lilian Rincon, said at the event that the new Siri AI will launch in English alongside the official release of iOS 27 (scheduled for September 14), with support for the following languages rolling out in October:

  • French
  • Japanese
  • Korean
  • Portuguese
  • Spanish

Rincon also confirmed two pieces of information that were first mentioned by Apple's Craig Federighi at this year's WWDC.

First, some features will have usage caps because they rely on powerful server-side models, and most iCloud+ plans will receive higher usage allowances.

Second, Apple Intelligence (of which Siri AI is only a part) will support the following 16 languages in this month's operating system updates:

  • English
  • Simplified Chinese
  • Traditional Chinese
  • Danish
  • Dutch
  • French
  • German
  • Italian
  • Japanese
  • Korean
  • Norwegian
  • Portuguese
  • Spanish
  • Swedish
  • Turkish
  • Vietnamese

Apple noted that Apple Intelligence is not available in China, but it appears the company is working behind the scenes to bring the features to that market. Apple also said Siri AI will not be available in China and the EU—the latter due to ongoing disagreements between Apple and regulators over the Digital Markets Act.
